extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and educators interested in humour theory and philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and interpret Thomas Hobbes's account of humour and laughter (the superiority theory), including its features, examples, and limitations. The page summarizes Hobbes's claims from The Elements of Law Natural and Politic (1650) for a non-specialist audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority theory of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes was a supporter of the superiority theory of humour and the first philosopher to directly refer to it; he was an uncompromising superiority theorist who believed that all humour and laughter is associated with conflict and competition and that laughter is an expression of a 'sudden glory' felt when becoming superior to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the central organizing claim: laughter signals a perceived superiority over others (or past selves). The page cites Hobbes's Elements of Law Natural and Politic (1650) as the source and positions him against other philosophers who only indirectly described the theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suddenness (sudden glory) as necessary feature
rubrics_metrics.description: The passion of laughter is 'nothing else but a sudden glory arising from sudden conception of some eminency in ourselves, by comparison with the infirmities of others, or with our own formerly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes emphasizes the suddenness of the feeling of superiority — it's the abrupt recognition of eminency that produces laughter. Examples and quotations are used to foreground suddenness as distinguishing laughable superiority from non-laughable feelings of superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour is tied to conflict and competition/power struggle
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes believed laughter assisted people in their struggle for power; humour and laughter are associated with conflict and competition and grounded in his broader theory of life ('State of Nature' and 'war of all against all').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article situates humour within Hobbes's political anthropology: laughter functions in social dominance and the contest for status, not merely as benign amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as malicious enjoyment (moral critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes proposed that laughter was a byproduct of our own malicious enjoyment experienced through our own sense of triumph over others; he viewed the use of humour at the expense of others (mocking, teasing) unfavourably and argued laughter should be suppressed and not used in excess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Hobbes's moral appraisal of many laugh-producing acts: they reflect malice or triumph and therefore have normative consequences (ought to be checked). The article contrasts this unforgiving account with more benign interpretations (e.g., Descartes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughing at others: comparison to perceived inferiority or absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: People laugh at the sudden realisation of the inferiority, absurdity or shortcomings of others when compared to their own perceived superiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains typical target-directed laughter: recognising another's folly or weakness relative to oneself produces sudden glory and thus laughter. The sudden recognition component is key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughing at oneself framed as superiority over past self
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-disparaging laughter is explained by Hobbes as laughing at a former, inferior version of oneself — one assigns superiority to the present self in comparison to the inferior past self.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a response to the counterargument that self-laughter defeats superiority theory; Hobbes treats it as consistent with the theory because the present self perceives superiority over an earlier state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughing at one's own joke arises from social power/feeling of superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: When someone laughs at their own joke, Hobbes would say they are laughing not at the joke itself but from the sense of superiority felt from telling the joke and the feelings of power they acquire from the social situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains self-amusement in social contexts as an expression of elevated social position or triumphant feeling rather than purely aesthetic appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour 'abstracted from persons' (absurdity and puns) challenges the theory
rubrics_metrics.description: There are examples of humour and laughter not associated with people (e.g., laughing at a word pun) or where no malice is present (e.g., a parent laughing at their baby) that complicate Hobbes's general claim that all laughter arises from superiority and conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page acknowledges these counterexamples as opening avenues to challenge Hobbes. It offers potential Hobbesian replies (e.g., superiority at understanding a pun, parental superiority over a baby) but notes Hobbes does a relatively poor job explaining benign humour.
